basic_information.official_title: AN ACT ADOPTING THE OFFICIAL HYMN OF THE BANGSAMORO AUTONOMOUS REGION IN MUSLIM MINDANAO
signed_by: Atty. Ali Pangalian M. Balindong, Speaker
Prof. Raby B. Angkal, Secretary General
basic_information.effectivity: 15 days after publication in a regional newspaper of general circulation

citizen_summary.what_is_this_about: Adopts the Bangsamoro Hymn, sets its official lyrics in full, requires every school and government office in the region to sing it at flag ceremonies — and, unusually for a symbols law, makes wilful violation a criminal offence.
citizen_summary.why_was_it_proposed: The Organic Law lets the region adopt its own hymn as an expression of self-governance. The act fixes the lyrics so the anthem cannot drift, and settles how and when it is sung.
citizen_summary.what_will_change: Schools, colleges, universities, public offices and government corporations must play and sing the hymn at flag-raising and flag-lowering ceremonies — always after the Philippine National Anthem, never before it. Arabic, English and Bangsamoro-language versions approved by the Chief Minister are equally official.
who_will_be_affected: Every school, college and university in the region — private as well as public
Public offices, government-owned or controlled corporations and other government instrumentalities
Bangsamoro offices located outside the area of autonomy
Anyone singing or performing the hymn, who is subject to the penalty clause
citizen_summary.when_will_it_take_effect: In force since 2020 — 15 days after publication.

what_this_means_for_you.in_short: NOW LAW. Schools and government offices must sing the Bangsamoro Hymn at flag ceremonies, always after the Philippine National Anthem. Unlike the flag and emblem laws, this one carries a fine of ₱50,000–₱100,000 and up to 6 months' imprisonment.
in_practice: The official lyrics are set out in full in the act itself
Rendition must follow the official musical arrangement and composition
Arabic, English, or any Bangsamoro language or dialect version approved by the Chief Minister is equally official
Required at flag-raising and flag-lowering ceremonies in schools, public offices, GOCCs and other government instrumentalities
The Philippine National Anthem must always be sung first
It may also be sung at ceremonial and symbolic functions and at private activities

for_specific_groups.Private schools: Section 5 names public and private schools, colleges and universities alike — the duty reaches institutions the government does not run.
for_specific_groups.Government offices: Required at both flag-raising and flag-lowering, including Bangsamoro offices sitting outside the region.
for_specific_groups.Musicians and performers: Rendition must accord with the official musical arrangement and composition, and the penalty clause applies to any person who wilfully violates any provision.
for_specific_groups.Non-Tagalog speakers: Arabic, English and any Bangsamoro language or dialect version approved by the Chief Minister counts as official.

what_this_means_for_you.where_this_applies: The BARMM, and Bangsamoro offices outside it.
what_this_means_for_you.when_you_will_feel_it: In force since 2020 — at every flag ceremony in a covered institution.
what_you_can_do: Sing the Philippine National Anthem first — the act requires the Bangsamoro Hymn always to follow it
Use the official arrangement, or an approved Arabic, English or Bangsamoro-language version
watch_out_for: The penalty applies to 'any person found willfully violating any provision of this Act', which is broad and undefined — the act does not say which acts amount to a violation.
The offence carries up to 6 months' imprisonment as well as a fine, at the court's discretion.
There is no defined process for approving an alternative-language version beyond the Chief Minister's approval.
The flag and emblem acts carry no penalty at all; this one does, which is a sharp inconsistency across the region's symbols laws.

key_terms_explained.Rendition: How the hymn is actually performed — the act requires it to follow the official musical arrangement and composition.
key_terms_explained.Alhamdulillah: 'Praise be to God' — the phrase that closes the hymn's refrain.
key_terms_explained.Wilfully: Deliberately rather than by accident. The penalty clause attaches to wilful violation.

what_this_means_for_you.status_note: Passed 30 January 2020, approved by the Chief Minister on 13 February 2020.

benefits.headline: An official anthem with fixed lyrics, and official versions in Arabic, English and Bangsamoro languages.

direct_benefits.benefit: Official lyrics published in the law itself
direct_benefits.how_to_access: Section 4 sets them out in full

direct_benefits.benefit: Equally official versions in Arabic, English, or a Bangsamoro language or dialect
direct_benefits.who_gets_it: Communities that do not use the original
direct_benefits.how_to_access: Subject to approval by the Chief Minister

indirect_benefits: A shared anthem at every flag ceremony in the region
The relationship with the national anthem settled in law rather than by custom
limitations: No funding for teaching or arrangement.
The penalty clause is broad and its triggers undefined.

for_schools_and_offices: Play and sing the hymn at flag-raising and flag-lowering ceremonies
Always sing the Philippine National Anthem first
Follow the official musical arrangement and composition
for_citizens: No duty to sing it — but the penalty clause reaches 'any person' who wilfully violates any provision.

what_is_prohibited: The act does not enumerate prohibited acts. Section 6 instead penalises any person found wilfully violating any provision — which on its face reaches a rendition departing from the official arrangement, or singing the hymn before the Philippine National Anthem.

penalties.for_citizens: Any person found wilfully violating any provision is, on conviction, punished by a fine of not less than ₱50,000 and not more than ₱100,000, or imprisonment of not more than 6 months, or both, at the discretion of the court.
penalties.note: This is the only one of the region's symbols acts to carry a penalty. The flag act (BAA 1) and the emblem act (BAA 2) create no offence at all.

where_to_complain.note: The act names no implementing body. Its penalty is enforced through the courts on conviction.

everyday_scenarios: A public school holds its Monday flag ceremony. It must play and sing the Philippine National Anthem first, then the Bangsamoro Hymn.
A private university in Maguindanao assumes the requirement applies only to public schools. It does not — Section 5 names private institutions expressly.
A community wants to sing the hymn in Maranao. A version in any Bangsamoro language or dialect is official once approved by the Chief Minister.
A performer rearranges the hymn for a concert. Section 5 requires rendition to accord with the official arrangement, and Section 6 penalises wilful violation of any provision.

key_provisions: Section 1 — Short title: the “Bangsamoro Hymn Act of 2020”.
Section 2 — Policy: in exercising its right to self-governance the region is free to adopt a hymn that conveys and preserves the peoples' identity, history, heritage and aspirations.
Section 3 — Adopts an Official Hymn of the BARMM pursuant to Article II, Section 2 of the Organic Law (RA 11054).

Section 4 — Sets out the official lyrics in full, opening 'Simula noon hanggang ngayon / Iisa ang naging layon' and closing on the refrain 'Bangsamoro'y tagumpay / Bunga ng pawis, dugo, at buhay / Kapayapaan, katarungan / Ay atin nang nakamtan / Alhamdulillah, Alhamdulillah / Pagpalain Bangsamoro'.

Section 5 — Rendition, whether played or sung, must accord with the official musical arrangement and composition. An Arabic, English, or any Bangsamoro language or dialect version approved by the Chief Minister is likewise official. All public and private schools, colleges and universities, public offices, government-owned or controlled corporations and other government instrumentalities in the Bangsamoro — and Bangsamoro offices outside the area of autonomy — are required to play and sing the hymn at flag-raising and flag-lowering ceremonies. It may also be sung at ceremonial and symbolic functions and private activities. Whenever it is sung it must always be preceded by the Philippine National Anthem.

Section 6 — Penalty: any person found wilfully violating any provision of the act shall, upon conviction, be punished by a fine of not less than ₱50,000 and not more than ₱100,000, or imprisonment of not more than 6 months, or both, at the discretion of the court.
Section 9 — Takes effect 15 days after publication in a regional newspaper of general circulation.

impact.figures_note: The act appropriates no funds. Its figures are penal: a fine of ₱50,000 to ₱100,000 and up to 6 months' imprisonment.

related_legislation.related_note: One of the first Parliament's four symbols acts, with the flag (BAA 1), the emblem (BAA 2) and the Parliament's own seal (BAA 16). It is the only one of them that creates an offence.

implementation_status.note: Read from the enacted text as signed. The official musical arrangement referred to in Section 5 is not reproduced in the signed copy, which sets out the lyrics only.

citizen_questions.q: When must the hymn be sung?
citizen_questions.a: At flag-raising and flag-lowering ceremonies in all public and private schools, colleges and universities, public offices, government corporations and other government instrumentalities in the region — and in Bangsamoro offices outside it.

citizen_questions.q: Does the Philippine National Anthem still come first?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. Section 5 says that whenever the Bangsamoro Hymn is sung it shall always be preceded by the singing of the Philippine National Anthem.

citizen_questions.q: Can it be sung in another language?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. An Arabic, English, or any Bangsamoro language or dialect version is likewise official, once approved by the Chief Minister.

Yes, and it is the only symbols act that has one. Wilfully violating any provision carries, on conviction, a fine of ₱50,000 to ₱100,000, or up to 6 months' imprisonment, or both, at the court's discretion.

citizen_questions.q: Can I sing it at a private event?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. Section 5 allows the hymn to be played and sung at ceremonial and symbolic functions and at private activities.
